en: When the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai speaks of the distinct contemplation of non-arising, he uses a mirror as a metaphor for the Dharma-realm and the eye as a metaphor for contemplative wisdom.
Blue, yellow, red, and white, as well as small, large, long, and short, serve as metaphors for the ten dharma-realms; blue specifically represents the causes and effects of the hells.

Yellow represents the causes and effects of hungry ghosts; red represents the causes and effects of animals; white represents the causes and effects of humans and devas; small forms represent the causes and effects of the two vehicles; large forms represent the causes and effects of bodhisattvas with supernatural powers; short forms represent the causes and effects of bodhisattvas of the distinct teaching; and long forms represent the causes and effects of Buddhas—all of these are distinguished within the mirror without error.
If one wishes to rectify oneself, one causes the nine types of causal conditions to not arise and the one type of causal condition to arise;
if one wishes to rectify others, one causes others' nine types of causal conditions to not arise and their one type of causal condition to arise.

Relying upon the *dharmadhātu*, one practices the bodhisattva path; sequentially employing the analytical wisdom of the essence (*tattva-vipaśyanā-jñāna*), one cuts off the four abodes of birth so that they do not arise.
Next, employing the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one cuts off adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) so that ignorance (*ajñāna*) does not arise.
Finally, employing the wisdom of ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*), one cuts off ignorance (*avidyā*) so that the root itself does not arise.

If the four abidings do not exist, then分段 (segmented birth) will not arise; if ignorance does not exist, then 方便 (expedient means) will not arise; if nescience does not exist, then 實報 (true retribution) will not arise. Birth is non-arising, and non-birth is also non-arising; therefore it is called "non-arising. This is termed the wisdom of non-arising according to the Separate Teaching.
Regarding the contemplation of the wisdom of non-arising according to the Perfect Teaching: one contemplates the perfect circle of the mirror;
one does not contemplate the back or the face, nor does one contemplate the reflected image. It is neither the back nor the dark, neither the face nor the light.
One does not grasp at various forms or appearances, nor does one grasp at various reflected images; one contemplates only the perfect circle, which has no boundaries and no beginning or end.
Regarding the absence of distinctions between unity and difference within the darkness of ignorance, this is likened to a perfect contemplation (*parivarta-vipaśyanā*):
one does not grasp at the appearances of the ten dharma-realms; there is neither good nor evil, neither heterodox nor orthodox, neither small nor great, and so forth.

All such things are extinguished, and one merely contemplates the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*), and the Buddha-dharma—whether it be form or fragrance, none are [grasped].
It is not a real characteristic; observing that afflictions, karma, and birth are themselves non-arising, and since non-arising does not arise, it is called "non-arising.
The suffering of the aggregates (skandhas), sense bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) is itself the Dharma-body; because it is not something manifested, it is named the Dharma-body.
Obstructions are themselves the Dharma-body, and greed, hatred, and delusion are themselves prajñā—not that which makes things clear.
Therefore it is named Prajñā; there is nothing for it to illuminate, as its nature is inherently lucid.
All karmic actions and fetters are termed "liberation," not because one attains release by severing bonds, nor because there is any substance to be bound, nor any binder.
Thus it is called liberation.

Liberation is the non-arising of karma; Prajñā is the non-arising of afflictions; the Dharma-body is the non-arising of suffering. These three non-arisings are one non-arising, and this one non-arising is the three non-arisings. Because they are neither three nor one, they are called "non-arising. How much more so for the transformational [body], whose afflictions, karma, and suffering are not non-arising?
This is precisely the wisdom of the perfect contemplation of non-arising, and so forth.
Regarding the fundamental and the manifested: Kātyāyana is fundamentally unborn from the very beginning; it is not that he is unborn only now.
Because he wishes to lead [beings] toward milk becoming curd, he is manifested as "non-arising" in the initial teaching.
Because milk is drawn forth to produce cream, its trace is the non-arising of the common;
because cream is drawn forth to produce curd, its trace is the non-arising of the distinct;
because curd is drawn forth to produce clarified butter, its trace is the non-arising of the perfect.
Yet its fundamental ground abides in the gateway of the letter A, meaning that all phenomena are originally unarisen.
If one hears the gateway of the letter A, one understands that all meanings are neither arisen nor unarisen;
yet, in manifesting traces to guide and transform beings, it can function as both arising and non-arising.

If sentient beings can realize the perfect non-arising, they will be identical to Ajñāta; being neither fundamental nor derivative, neither arising nor non-arising, the great causal conditions for their enlightenment will here be consummated.
Therefore, the subsequent text says:
"Pūrṇa, if I were to fully describe all these various manifestations, sentient beings who heard them would harbor doubts and confusion in their minds."
This is precisely the meaning thereof. The *Āgama* states:
"Ānanda followed behind the Buddha holding a parasol and a lamp; the Great Brahmā King followed behind Cunda holding a parasol and a lamp."
All of these demonstrate the provisional traces in order to reveal the fundamental reality.
As for observing that the mind does not arise, this can be understood through the non-arising of the three contemplations; there is no need to elaborate further.

“Mahākāśyapa” is translated here as “Great Kūrma” (Great Turtle Clan). His ancestors practiced the Way, and a divine tortoise appeared bearing a diagram of the immortals; because his clan was named after this virtue, he is called of the Kūrma (Turtle) Clan.

The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha translated it as "Light-Wave" (Guāngbō). Because the bodily radiance of the ancient seer surged forth with such brilliance that it could eclipse all other lights so they would no longer appear, it is called "Light-Wave.
It is also called "Drinker of Light" (Yǐnguāng), for Kāśyapa’s bodily radiance was likewise able to outshine other objects.
He was named Pippala, or Pippalāyana, or Tivili. This refers to the *pippala* tree;
because his parents prayed to the tree deity and obtained this son, they named him after the tree.
The son of the Vṛji was born in this village, and people took that as his name; his family was very wealthy.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:

"In Rājagṛha there was a great wealthy householder named Kapila; his wife’s name was Dhanā, his son’s name was Piṣpalaka, and his daughter-in-law’s name was Bhadrā. His household was a thousand times more prosperous than that of King Bimbisāra, such that none of the sixteen great kingdoms could rival them as neighbors."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Dharmakośa*) states:

"After the parinirvāṇa of Vipaśyin Buddha, the golden images and stupas fell into disrepair. At that time, there was a poor woman who begged for a gold bead and requested a craftsman to fashion it into a thin plate."
The goldsmith, filled with joy, finished polishing and refining the Buddha’s image, and they made a vow to become husband and wife.

For ninety-one kalpas, their bodies were always golden in color among humans and devas, and their minds constantly experienced bliss. Finally, he was conceived in the womb of a brahmin named Nyagrodha in the kingdom of Magadha. Fearing that King Bimbisāra might punish him for his transgression, he reduced the number of plows by one, using only nine hundred and ninety-nine pairs of oxen for his golden plow.
Furthermore, a sutra states:

"In that household there is cotton cloth (*karpāsa*), even the lowest grade of which is worth a hundred thousand taels of gold; if it is driven seven feet into the ground with a nail, the cloth does not tear or break, remaining no different from its original state."
"Sixty storehouses of gold and grain; one storehouse has a capacity of three hundred and forty *hu*.
A "storehouse" (*ku*) is a type of granary.
Furthermore, a sutra states:
"By offering barley rice to a Pratyekabuddha, one enjoys happiness for a thousand rebirths each in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; such a person possesses thirty marks. To speak directly of golden color:

the gold of Jambūnada, though at the bottom of turbid water, has its radiance penetrate through the water; in the dark, it is extinguished by darkness. Yet the bodily radiance of Kāśyapa surpasses this gold, his bodily light illuminating a distance of one yojana."
The absence of two marks likely refers to the lack of the *ūrṇā* (white tuft) and the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance).
Therefore, when the gods requested the compilation of the scriptures, they praised him, saying:
"The Elder has eliminated desire, anger, and pride; his form is like a pillar of purple-gold. From top to bottom he is majestic and sublime beyond compare; his eyes are clear and pure like a lotus."

Abandoning this household business, he further took a wife of golden hue who lay with him without desire; then, renouncing it all, he left the home life. He took his priceless robes and cut them to make a saṃghāṭī, folding them four times to offer as a seat for the Buddha. Thus, these three acts of renunciation were peerless in the world; this is called "great renunciation."

In the village of Vajji, he encountered the Buddha and offered him a precious robe; the Buddha, in turn, bestowed upon him a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe). This robe was the great sage’s own outer robe, and it was neither coarse nor heavy.
Therefore, Kāśyapa said: "When I receive the Buddha’s robe, I regard it as my teacher and as a stūpa; I have never used it as a pillow for my head, much less covered myself with it while lying down."
"Such a great robe greatly advances my practice.
Therefore, it is called "receiving the great.
Among the disciples of the Buddha, many were named Kāśyapa; such as the Ten Powers and the Three Kāśyapas, all of whom were great beings.
Because he was the eldest among those who shared his name, he was designated as Mahākāśyapa.

While in the village of Vajji, he first heard from the Buddha concerning the superior training in higher morality, concentration, and wisdom; he immediately attained the state free from outflows (*anāsrava*), undertook the practice of alms-gathering, and observed the twelve *dhūta* ascetic practices. Even as he grew old, he did not abandon them. Later, the Buddha said to him: "Your years are advanced;

you may now relinquish the practice of alms-gathering and return to the community to receive food. You may relinquish your coarse, heavy rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*) and accept light, dyed garments from laypeople."
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:

"If the Buddha does not appear in the world, I shall become a pratyekabuddha and practice the dhūta austerities for the rest of my life. I do not dare now to abandon what I have practiced to learn anything else; furthermore, I wish to serve as a light for future generations."
"In a future age, they will say:
'The Elder Kāśyapa was praised by the Buddha; I, too, shall practice difficult and painful austerities. The Buddha said:
“Excellent! This constitutes the greatness of practice. *Ekottarika Āgama*:
"Among those who practice the twelve dhūtas and perform difficult ascetic practices within the Buddha-dharma, Mahākāśyapa is foremost.
Having practiced these dhūtas for a long time, his hair and beard grew long and his robes were tattered; when he came to where the Buddha was, the bhikṣus gave rise to arrogance."
The Buddha commanded him to take half of the Buddha’s seat and sit together with him, but Kāśyapa was unwilling.
The Buddha said:
"I possess the four dhyānas; through meditative concentration, my mind is stilled and remains without depletion from beginning to end, and it is the same for Kāśyapa."
I possess great loving-kindness that covers all beings, and you likewise possess this same nature of loving-kindness;
I possess great compassion that delivers sentient beings, and you are likewise so;
I possess the four divine samādhis:
First, formlessness; second, immeasurable intention; third, pure accumulation; fourth, non-retrogression—you are also thus.
I possess the six supernormal powers, and you are also thus.
I possess the four meditative concentrations:
"First, meditative concentration; second, wisdom-concentration; third, insight-concentration; fourth, precept-concentration—you are also like this. The *Ekottarika Āgama* says:
"A certain Brahmin addressed the Buddha:"
"Yesterday a brahmin came to my house; who was he?
The Buddha pointed to Kāśyapa.
He asked again:
"This ascetic is not a brāhmaṇa.
The Buddha said, "I know the laws and teachings of the ascetics as well as those of the brāhmaṇas; Kāśyapa knows them just as I do."
“Kāśyapa’s merit is no different from my own; for what reason does he not sit?
When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s praise, their hearts were struck with awe and their hair stood on end.

The Buddha then recounted the original causes and conditions: In the past, there was a noble king named Mandhātṛ, whose talent was peerless. The Lord of Devas, admiring his virtue, sent a chariot drawn by a thousand horses to the palace gate to welcome the king. The Lord of Devas went out to meet him and sat together with the king; after they had enjoyed each other’s company, he escorted the king back to his palace.

In the past, Kāśyapa invited me to share his seat of birth and death; now that I have attained Buddhahood, I repay his former kindness by offering him the Seat of the True Dharma. When he sat opposite the Buddha, gods and humans alike declared him the Teacher of the Buddha.
Furthermore, while Kāśyapa was preaching the Dharma for the bhikṣuṇīs together with Ānanda, there was one bhikṣuṇī who did not approve and said:
"It is like a needle-seller selling needles before a master needle-maker."
Kāśyapa said to Ānanda,
"This bhikṣuṇī regards you as her needle-maker, while she regards me as a peddler of needles.
Kāśyapa then spoke to the bhikṣuṇī:
"The Buddha spoke the *Candropama-sūtra*, saying that one should increase [in virtue] day by day, always like a novice; did you not hear this, Mahākāśyapa?
He shared half his seat with you amidst the great assembly; did you not hear this?"
"In the midst of the great assembly, you praised his vast merits as being equal to those of the Buddha; did you not hear this?
How can such a person be called a 'needle-seller'?
Such instances demonstrate that he was highly esteemed and approved by the Buddha.

Regarding "great in rank": he was great among the great assembly; he was great among the twelve hundred and fifty [monks]; he was great among the five hundred; he was great among the four great disciples; he served as the abbot of the five mountain monasteries and acted as the presiding *sthavira* for the affairs of Jambudvīpa; therefore, it is said that his rank was great.

After the Buddha’s cremation, four *pātra* trees grew from the site of the ashes; this symbolizes that Kāśyapa compiled the teachings of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* into the Tripiṭaka and the Four Āgamas.
Sengzhao’s preface states:

"The ultimate principle transcends all designations; thus the worthy and sages remain in profound silence. Yet the mysterious purport cannot be transmitted without words; thus Śākyamuni established his teaching through them."

"Restrain body and speech through the prohibitions and precepts; clarify good and evil by guiding them with the Sūtras; and expound the profound and subtle by analyzing them through the Dharma-lakṣaṇas.
This refers precisely to the clarification of the Three Piṭakas: Vinaya, Sūtra, and Abhidharma.

The *Ekottarika-āgama* clarifies the causes and effects of humans and devas; the *Dīrgha-āgama* refutes false views; the *Madhyama-āgama* elucidates profound meanings; and the *Saṃyukta-āgama* clarifies meditative concentration—all of these are the achievements of Mahākāśyapa.

If one were to discuss the compilation separately, Ānanda recited the Sūtras, Upāli recited the Vinaya, and Kāśyapa recited the Abhidharma; therefore, it is said that the Great Compilation was performed.
After the Tathāgata’s departure, the Dharma was entrusted to Kāśyapa, who is able to serve as a refuge for all beings just like the Tathāgata himself.
Why is this? If there are those who practice the ascetic dhūta austerities, my Dharma will endure.
If this person did not exist, my Dharma would not endure.

Kāśyapa was able to shoulder the Buddha-Dharma and cause it to remain for a long time, until the coming of the future Buddha; having completed the entrustment of the Dharma and the transmission of the robe, he then entered parinirvāṇa. Therefore, he is said to be "great in upholding the Dharma."
Then Kāśyapa, having ascended invisibly to heaven to pay homage to the Buddha’s hair-relics, preached the Dharma to the devas, saying:
"By doing good one is born in heaven; by committing evil one enters the abyss. The five desires are impermanent, like dew upon a flower that withers at the touch of the sun."
Thereupon, they departed separately.
The devas wept and sighed, saying:

"To those who were destitute in their villages and lanes, suffering, afflicted, weak, poor, and orphaned—He always felt compassion for them. Now that He abandons us to enter parinirvāṇa, who will again provide protection?"

Thus it is said. According to the teaching, this clarifies "shaking off" (*vidhūnana*); one shakes off twelve kinds of faults: namely, there is suffering when seeking fine clothes, much fear when obtaining them, and the arising of vexation when losing them.
The paṃsukūla robe is free from the five fears of water, fire, thieves, robbers, and royal oppression;
if one were to possess many robes, the labor required for sewing, mending, and washing would also be great, therefore one wears only the three robes.
Furthermore, if one eats within the saṃgha, one must attend to monastic affairs; therefore, one practices alms-gathering.
If one accepts leftover food or light snacks, it will disturb the mind and cause the loss of the proper time for practice; therefore, one eats in a single sitting.

Eating too much is difficult to digest and gives rise to sleepiness and indolence, while eating too little leads to hunger and a lack of strength; therefore, one observes moderation in the amount of food.
Carrying and washing many vessels creates numerous obstacles; therefore, one eats from a single bowl.
Because one is weary of the exertion of labor, one does not drink gruel;
because of attachment to dwellings, one dwells under trees;
and because of attachment even to dwelling under trees, one dwells in cemeteries.
One dwells in the open air because the grief and sorrow associated with dwelling among tombs are obstructive;
one remains constantly seated because lying down diminishes merit and increases indolence.
Two are rules concerning clothing, six are rules concerning food, and four are rules concerning the dwelling place.

Furthermore, taking alms-seeking as an illustration to clarify "shaking off" (the defilements): when food is easily obtained, joy arises; when it is difficult to obtain, anger arises. To receive what is good is attachment; to receive what is bad is sorrow. Sorrow and joy arise based on form (*rūpa*), which is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Experiencing this sorrow and joy is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*). Grasping the characteristics of sorrow and joy is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*). Sorrow and joy themselves are the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*). Discriminating between sorrow and joy is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

Sorrow and joy are the two bases of mind and mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) within the three realms; these realms, bases, and aggregates are themselves the Truth of Suffering. To think, "I am able to beg for alms," and to calculate in terms of self or non-self—taking begging as the path and begging as reality—is to regard it as such a truth.

To praise those who rejoice and revile those who are angry, to be able to endure being rebuked yet harbor doubt, and to fail to understand—these constitute ignorance (*moha*). These are the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*); when they are applied across the three realms and the four noble truths, they are termed the eighty-eight proclivities of the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).

If consciousness, within the context of seeking alms, is covered by a continuous succession resembling the four perversions—deeming things permanent because they are pleasing to the mind, deeming them pleasant because of the concealment of their shifting activities, deeming them self because of the covering of thin skin, and deeming them pure—it is through this consciousness that the four coverings exist yet the four perversions are absent. By diligently warding off the two evils and giving rise to the two virtues, one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness, the five faculties, the five powers, and the factors of enlightenment; this is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

In the practice of begging for alms, when one does not conceive of a self, delusion (*moha*) ceases; because delusion ceases, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) ceases; because craving ceases, aversion (*dveṣa*) ceases; because aversion ceases, one does not exalt oneself and thus pride (*māna*) ceases; because pride ceases, there is no doubt when being rebuked; because there is no self, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) ceases; because the view of a self ceases, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) ceases; by not clinging to this as the path, the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) ceases; by not reckoning things as real, the attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) ceases; and by not holding false attachments, wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) ceases. Through the cessation of these ten, the eighty-eight [afflictions] cease; through the cessation of the eighty-eight, the fetters of the cause (*hetu-bandhana*) cease; through the cessation of the fetters of the cause, the fetters of the fruit (*phala-bandhana*) cease; and through the cessation of the fetters of the fruit, the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) cease. This is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
If, amidst the practice of alms-gathering, one does not perceive the Four Noble Truths, for this reason one wanders for a long time in the great ocean of suffering of birth and death;
if one can perceive the Four Truths, then one attains the cessation of birth and death.
Once birth and death have been exhausted, one will no longer undergo further existence; this is the wisdom of the contemplation of shaking off [defilements] within the practice of alms-gathering.
The same applies to the rules for robes and the rules for dwellings.

These are the three types of *dhūta* (ascetic purification) according to the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa*). As for the practitioner who shakes off [defilements] through this teaching: taking the realization of reality and the attainment of tranquility as their dwelling place; taking the wisdom of emptiness as their food; and taking the practice of emptying the mind while performing all deeds as their clothing—since the nature of all things is eternally empty and there is no time when it is not empty, they shake off all things with the wisdom of emptiness, seeing them all as like illusions and transformations. Because deluded thoughts and all evils are extinguished and do not arise, and because the various mental states and mental factors do not function—due to their being ungraspable—the concentration on emptiness among all concentrations is the foremost; ascetic practice among all ascetic practices is the foremost; and the shaking-off by means of the wisdom of emptiness among all forms of shaking-off is the most supreme.

The brief exposition is concluded. Regarding the specific teaching on "shaking off" (dhūta): one takes the Dharma-body as the place of dwelling, takes Prajñā-wisdom as food, and uses all various practices as adornments and coverings. These coverings shake off the evil of black karma; Prajñā shakes off the evil of afflictions; and the Dharma-body shakes off the suffering of birth and death. First, one shakes off the afflictions, karma, and suffering of the segmented [birth-and-death]; next, one shakes off the afflictions, karma, and suffering of the transformative [birth-and-death]. This is the dhūta of the Middle Way’s correct contemplation, which transcends the ascetic practices performed by the Two Vehicles, and so forth.

Regarding the "shaking off" (dhūta) of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): one’s dwelling is itself clothing and food; yet, while it is but a single dharma, it is explained as three through differentiation. One shaking off is all shaking off, and all shaking off is one shaking off. It is neither one nor many; within all shaking off, there is nothing that is not the true mark (dharmatā). This is the practice of all Buddhas, the Tathāgata-practice, which transcends the practices of all bodhisattvas and is pure, and so forth.

Regarding "original and trace" (*honji*): the original [state] shares with the Tathāgata the principle of ultimate emptiness, attains the same vast Dharma-body, attains the same unimpeded wisdom, and attains the same immeasurable merit. Internally, it has abandoned attachment to dharmas; externally, it is free from defilement. Having shaken off all impurities both within and without, the original state is already pure. Now, wishing to extract the essence of milk, one shakes it within the realm of phenomena; next, to extract the essence of curd, one shakes it within the realm of emptiness; next, to extract the essence of fresh butter, one shakes it within the realm of differentiation; and finally, to extract the essence of refined butter, one shakes it within the realm of perfection.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: through the *emptiness* (śūnyatā) aspect, one shakes off grasping at signs; through the *provisional* (prajñapti) aspect, one shakes off the sands of delusion; through the *middle* (madhyama) aspect, one shakes off ignorance; and within the single mind, one shakes off the five stages of dwelling, and so forth.
Regarding the "Three Kāśyapas," *Kāśyapa* is explained as before.
"Uruvilvā" is also *Uruvī*, or *Uve*; this is translated as "Pumpkin Grove."
"Nadi" is translated here as "river" or "stream.
"Gayā" is also rendered as "Gaya" or "Elephant," and is translated as "City-Home.
It is located seven *yojanas* south of Rājagṛha. During the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, they jointly erected a sacrificial pillar there, and on that account, they became brothers.
The elder brother was the teacher of King Bimbisāra, with five hundred disciples;
each of his two younger brothers had two hundred and fifty, and they practiced the Dharma of their elder brother.
The Buddha performed ten kinds of miraculous transformations:

It is said that he was not struck by dragon venom, not burned by dragon fire, and not drowned in the Ganges River; he took fruit from the three directions and rice from the north, and the nectar of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Knowing they harbored suspicions, he would vanish; knowing they were mindful of him, he would appear. Fire could not extinguish him, and axes could not descend once raised. He manifested many such auspicious signs.

Yet, despite witnessing these various transformations, his heterodox attachments remained unaltered; thus it was said: "Though Gautama possesses such spiritual powers, he is not equal to the truth of my Way."
The Buddha then said to him,
"You are not an Arhat, nor have you attained the Way. At these words,
he was suddenly enlightened, and both master and disciple were humbled.
The two younger brothers, seeing these signs, also followed him back to the Buddha; these constitute the one thousand bhikṣus.
Regarding the provisional teaching, as the *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa is foremost in being able to protect the fourfold assembly and provide them with the four requisites so that they lack for nothing."
The bhikṣu Nadi was serene in mind, having subdued all fetters, and was foremost in diligence;
the bhikṣu Gaya had thoroughly contemplated all dharmas and was entirely without attachment, being foremost in his skillful ability to teach and transform others.
This is the intended meaning within the teaching on curd.
If one progresses to the stage of fresh butter (*navanīta*), one should then feel shame for the small and aspire to the great; this principle may be understood by analogy.
If one progresses to the stage of matured butter (*ghṛta*), one should then abandon worldly activities and receive the teachings.
If one proceeds to enter the *amṛta* (the supreme essence), it is as in this sutra where one receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) of attaining Buddhahood.

Regarding the "original" and the "traces": one abides in the three virtues; the forest is *prajñā*, the city is the *dharmakāya*, and the water is *vimukti*. This constitutes the secret original treasury;
yet the traces rely upon the forest, city, and water to deliver sentient beings.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: it is to correctly contemplate the nature of the mind as the Middle Way, unmoving like a city wall defending against enemies; unmoving yet moving, like water purifying all peripheral delusions; and illuminating both decay and flourishing simultaneously, like a lush and verdant forest. These three dharmas supporting one another are like brothers joined by the same branch.

“Śāriputra”—if one were to provide the full form, it should be called Śāriputra; this translates as “Son of Śārī. Furthermore, *śārī* can be translated as “pearl”: because his mother was the most intelligent among women, and since the mark of intelligence resides in the pupils of the eyes, he is a “pearl” born from those eyes.
Alternatively, it translates as “Son of Śārī”: because this woman possessed a beautiful physical form, and he was born from her body, he is thus called the “Son of Śārī.”
At that time, people designated him with this title to honor his mother by means of her son.

His father gave him the name Upatisya (or Upatissa), which translates as "Discourse on Meaning" (*Arthaviniścaya*). He obtained his wife through such discourse, and his son was named after it; thus, the name serves to commemorate the virtues of his father.
The *Śāstra* states:
"My name is Tiṣya; following my name, a title was made for me, namely Upatiṣya.

*Upa* here means "following," while *Tiṣya* is the name of a star. Furthermore, *śe* indicates the father and *li* indicates the mother; because both parents are manifested together, he is called Śāriputra.
Pūrṇa was his son.
His clan name was Kauṣṭhila, and he was of the Brahmin caste.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"In my Buddha-dharma, Śāriputra is foremost among those whose wisdom is inexhaustible and who resolve all doubts.

Formerly, as stated in the *Sheng jing* (Sūtra on Past Lives), in the past, an uncle and his nephew were both weavers; knowing of the king's treasure storehouse, they dug into the earth to steal it and obtained a great quantity of precious jewels.
The Jewel Overseer informed the King, who said, "Do not raise an alarm; that thief will soon arrive. Wait and seize him.
Consequently, the nephew ordered his uncle to enter, whereupon he was captured. Fearing that others might recognize him, the nephew immediately beheaded his uncle.

The King ordered that the corpse be placed at a crossroads to summon its kinsmen; later, taking advantage of a large and noisy gathering of merchants, the nephew loaded two carts with firewood and covered it over.
The king again had him captured; furthermore, while the boy was dancing and playing, he threw him into a fire to burn him.
On another occasion, the king hosted a banquet; when the guards were heavily intoxicated, he took the wine jars, filled them with bones, and departed.
Fearing their craftiness, the king sent his daughter out with strict guards to the water's edge. He first instructed his daughter: "Should anyone come, seize them and call for me.
As they were floating logs upon the water, the guards took them for people; but when they looked closely, they were merely logs.
Being unprepared for days on end, he was thus able to approach the woman.
The woman seized his garment, whereupon he immediately handed her a dead man’s hand and departed. The woman cried out loudly; when she looked at it, it was indeed a dead man’s hand.
Because of this, she conceived and gave birth to a handsome son.
The king ordered a wet nurse to carry him out, whereupon those who were crying seized him.

After several days of hunger and thirst, they came beneath a stove for baking cakes; the baker gave them some cakes, and they cried again. The king ordered them out once more. Thereafter, they sold strong wine and waited until people were deeply intoxicated, then carried the child away and crossed into another country.

A neighboring state admired his stratagem and offered him the daughter of its high minister as a wife; however, he did not accept this, instead adopting the name "E'r" (Child). Subsequently, the King of his own country promised him his daughter in marriage.

Suspecting that he might be the former thief, the man set out with five hundred horsemen—each equipped with saddles, horses, and garments identical to those of the others—to go and welcome the bride. When the King saw him, he asked if he was the former thief; sighing at his craftiness and deceit, he gave him his daughter in marriage.
The nephew was Śāriputra, and the uncle was Devadatta, and so forth.

As for the fetus: his father’s name was Upatiṣya, who was learned in the classics. He bound his belly with iron plates and wore a crown of fire upon his head; he walked alone through Rājagṛha, beating the drum of debate. The State Preceptor Dāruka, knowing that [the child] would surpass him and perceiving the inauspicious signs, was defeated in argument and stripped of his fief, and subsequently gave his daughter to him in marriage.
His wife dreamed that a man clad in armor, holding a vajra in his hand, shattered all the mountains and then stood beside one remaining mountain.
Upon waking, she felt her body heavy and questioned her husband. Her husband said:
"That which you carry in your womb will shatter all masters of treatises; it will only fail to overcome one person, who shall become your disciple."
The uncle’s name was Kauṣṭhila; he had always prevailed in debate over his sister, but now that she bore a wise man, her arguments surpassed those of her nephew.
The nephew thought to himself:

"This is not due to my sister's own power; it must be that a wise person has entered her womb and lent his eloquence to her mouth. If this is so even while he is still in the womb, how much more so once he is born?"
Having left his home to travel extensively for further study, he had no leisure to trim his nails; thus, people of the time called him the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (Long-Nail), and so forth.
The two nāgas, Nanda and Upananda, protected the city of Rājagṛha, sending down rain at the proper times, so that the kingdom never suffered from years of famine.

The King, along with his ministers and subjects, held a great assembly every year, arranging three high seats for the King, the Crown Prince, and the Master of Treatises (Śāstrin). When Śāriputra reached the age of eight, he went to the assembly hall and asked people about the three seats. When they had answered him fully, he immediately rose above the crowd and ascended the debating throne. The assembly of scholars were all ashamed and refused to engage in debate, thinking, "To defeat this child would bring no credit;
yet if we fail him, the humiliation would be immense!"
He dispatched all his attendants to deliver messages and inquire about him.
Each time they returned with their reports, [the opponent] would completely topple all the banners, and none dared to face him.
The king, along with his ministers and subjects, celebrated with boundless joy, for it was said that peace was approaching for the kingdom and a wise man had appeared in the world.

By the age of sixteen, he had thoroughly mastered all the scriptures of Jambudvīpa; there was nothing in which he was not proficient. He was erudite in both antiquity and the present, elucidating the most profound and abstruse matters. In debate, he was peerless among the sixteen great nations and was preeminent throughout the five regions of India.

He served as a disciple under the brahmin Śāraṇa; he mastered all the brahmin’s arts and techniques. The teacher had two hundred and fifty disciples, all of whom followed Śāriputra and were brought to completion by him.
As Śāriputra was about to die, he smiled with joy. When Mahāmaudgalyāyana asked for the reason, he replied:

"Worldly people lack the eye of wisdom and are thus attached to the intimacy of affection. I saw the King of Kāñcanamālā die, and his queen cast herself into a mass of fire, vowing to be reborn in the same place as him."
Having said this, his life came to an end.
Later, he encountered a merchant from Suvarṇabhūmi and, upon questioning him, found it to be exactly as he had said.
Śāriputra then felt deep remorse.
"I have not yet exhausted my teacher's skill, yet he did not transmit this Dharma to me; was it because I am not the right vessel, or was the teacher withholding it?
Realizing that he had not yet attained mastery, he sought an even more excellent Dharma, but found no teacher to serve.
Although he did not yet master this one teaching, he was proficient in all other teachings and was the foremost among the assembly of non-Buddhists.
While on the road, he saw Aṅgulimāla’s dignified and composed demeanor, and thus asked about his teacher’s doctrine. Aṅgulimāla replied:
"All phenomena arise from conditions; therefore they are called 'dependent origination. This is the teaching on conditions and their cessation—this is what my teacher has taught."
Upon hearing this once, he immediately attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. He came to the Buddha’s presence and, within seven days, thoroughly mastered the ocean-like depths of the Buddha-dharma.
It is further said that fifteen days later he attained *arhatship*, becoming the preceptor for Rāhula, the teacher for Gavāmpati, and a right-hand disciple among the assembly of *śrāvakas*.
Devadatta split the Sangha and led away five hundred bhikṣus; Śāriputra went to convert them, and they all returned, and so forth.
When Raudrākṣa competed in strength with Śāriputra, Raudrākṣa became a flower pond and Śāriputra became an elephant that pulled out the flowers and trampled the pond;
Raudrākṣa became a yakṣa ghost and Śāriputra became King Vaiśravaṇa.
All [their] various [qualities] are supreme; they deliver, distinguish, and subdue.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states:
"Śāriputra is the mother who gave birth to the fourfold assembly, while Maudgalyāyana is the foster mother... and so forth.
The second fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* states:

"The bhikṣus dwelling in their place of birth praised Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra for his fewness of desires, contentment, diligence, seclusion, single-mindedness, right mindfulness, and untainted wisdom; they also exhorted others and spoke in praise of these same qualities."
At that time, Śāriputra heard this and thought:
"When shall I see this person? When will this person arrive at the Buddha's dwelling?"
The other pointed out, saying:
"The one with a white, broad face, a prominent nose, and a parrot-like beak—such is his physical appearance.
Later, they met at the Andhavana (translated here as "Victorious Forest"), where Śāriputra asked:
"Does the worthy one practice the holy life under Gautama? He replied: "It is so."
He asked again:
"Is it for the sake of purifying the precepts and practicing the holy life? He replied:

"No. "Is it for the sake of purification of mind, purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision that one cultivates the holy life?"
He replied, "No. He asked again:
"If you previously said 'it is so,' yet now say 'it is not,' what is the meaning of this? He replied:
‘One cultivates the holy life for the sake of nirvana without remainder.
He asked again:
‘Is it because of the purity of precepts that there is nirvana without remainder?’
He replied, “No.
And so on, until: “Because the knowledge of the path has been abandoned and purified, would there still be nirvana without remainder?”
He replied: "No. He asked again:
"What is the meaning of this? He replied:

"If, by means of the purity of precepts, one speaks of 'without remainder' even when there is still remainder, this is a case of calling 'with remainder' 'without remainder. This applies even up to the purity of the knowledge and abandonment of the path of entry; even if there is still remainder, it is called 'without remainder.'"
If one were to be separated from these seven, ordinary persons would attain parinirvāṇa, because ordinary persons are separated from these seven.

Because they are not separated [from them], there is the purification of virtue, up to the purification of mind, and even the purification of the knowledge of the path and the abandonment [of defilements].
Virtuous one, listen as I speak a parable.

Suppose King Prasenajit wished to travel from Kauśala to Vātikā; he would station seven chariots along the way, discarding the first to board the second, and so on, until discarding the sixth to board the seventh.
The people of Vārāṇasī asked,
"Did you ride the first chariot?
He replied:
"No. [The question continues] "up to riding in the seventh chariot.
The answer is:
"No. Question: "Is it apart from these seven chariots?"
Answer: "No. This metaphorical question may be understood accordingly.
Śāriputra asked: "What is your name, O worthy one, and how do your fellow practitioners in the holy life address you?
He replied:
"My father's name was Pūrṇa and my mother's name was Maitrāyaṇī; those who practice the holy life call me Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Śāriputra praised him, saying: "Excellent!"

The worthy Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra is a disciple of the Tathāgata; he is wise, eloquent, intelligent, resolute, secure, and fearless. Having attained great eloquence and grasped the banner of the Deathless, he has personally realized the Deathless. Those who encounter him obtain great benefit; all fellow practitioners of the holy life should wrap their robes around his head and carry him upon it.
Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra asked:
"Venerable one, what is your name, and how are you addressed by your fellow practitioners of the holy life? He replied:
"My father's name was Upatiṣya and my mother's name was Śārī; therefore, I am called Śāriputra. Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra sighed and said:

"Now, one might debate with the disciples of the World-Honored One and not know [the answer]; one might debate with a second World-Honored One and not know; one might debate with the General of the Dharma and not know; and one might debate with the one who turns the wheel of the Dharma and again with his disciple, and still not know."
"If I knew that the Venerable One could not answer even a single phrase, much less this profound discourse, [I would have desisted].
Excellent! Excellent!"
"To become a disciple of the Tathāgata, one must even wrap one's robe around one's head and carry it upon it," and so forth.

When the Buddha spoke a single phrase, Śāriputra took that single phrase as his foundation and, for seven days and seven nights, let out a lion’s roar, producing ever-new phrases and flavors without end. How much more so when the Buddha speaks extensively—how could the wisdom and eloquence of Śāriputra ever be exhausted?
The *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle 20, states:
"When the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta, a nāga king said:
'This assembly does not see Śāriputra; we pray that the Buddha will summon him.'"
The Buddha commanded Maudgalyāyana to go to the Jetavana and summon him; at that time, Śāriputra was sewing his five-layered rag robe.
He replied, "You may go on ahead; I shall follow later."
Maudgalyāyana said, "I am a messenger of the Buddha; how can I go on ahead?
Maudgalyāyana rubbed his robe with his hand, and the robe was instantly restored.
Śāriputra thought, "Maudgalyāyana is testing me; I shall test him in turn.
He immediately threw his robe-string to the ground and said, "Are you able to lift this?"
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself,
"Śāriputra is testing me.
He then exerted all his strength, yet he could not lift it.
At that time, Śāriputra tied a rope to a jambu tree, and one world-system shook;
when he tied it to two, three, or four trees, even the four-continent world-system could not remain stable;

furthermore, when he tied it to the small thousand, middle thousand, and great thousand world-systems, they likewise could not remain stable; yet when he tied it to the legs of the Buddha’s seat in other directions, all the Buddha-worlds in the ten directions remained utterly motionless.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"My supernatural powers are foremost; if I cannot move this now, have I lost my powers?
He therefore urged [the Buddha] to depart, to which [the Buddha] replied:
"Go ahead first.
Maudgalyāyana returned to the Buddha's presence and saw Śāriputra already there before the Buddha.
When the Dragon King asked the Buddha about the earthquake, the Buddha replied:
"By the power of two.
The Dragon King and the five hundred bhikṣus conceived a sense of contempt toward Maudgalyāyana. The Buddha said:

"Śāriputra has attained mastery over the four spiritual powers, and Maudgalyāyana likewise possesses such mastery; yet that he was unable to pull [the mountain] out was solely due to the power of the Buddha."
He said to Maudgalyāyana, "Display your supernatural power.

Maudgalyāyana placed five hundred bhikṣus in his alms-bowl carrier and lifted them up to the Brahma palace; with one foot treading upon Mount Sumeru and the other reaching the Brahma palace, while his body remained in that location, he recited verses that filled the great trichiliocosm, causing the hearts of the five hundred to be subdued, and so forth.

Regarding the teaching by restriction (*yuejiao*): if the wisdom of the Tripitaka is precisely the ten knowledges of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it severs the fetters, realizes the truth, and assists the Buddha in propagating the transformation.
This is the meaning of the passage in the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) at fascicle 40, which refers to him as the "Great General on the Right."

Regarding the wisdom of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*), as explained in the *Prajñāpāramitā* itself concerning why one is called a Mahāsattva: it is because one destroys such views as the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*), the view of a Buddha (*buddha-dṛṣṭi*), the view of bodhi (*bodhi-dṛṣṭi*), and the view of turning the wheel of Dharma (*dharma-cakra-pravartana-dṛṣṭi*); for this reason, one is named a Mahāsattva.

The various noble ones (ārya) speak of their own Dharma; it is not like the arbitrary claims made by people today. One should know that Śāriputra did not merely destroy views of birth-and-death (saṃsāra), but also destroyed views of the Buddha, bodhi, the wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), and nirvāṇa. This wisdom differs from that of the initial teaching.

Regarding the wisdom of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*), it should be distinguished by means of the five flavors. If, from the very beginning, one hears only of milk and curd but not the other flavors, and one resolves to practice and practices only milk and curd, this is the wisdom of the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*).

If one hears only of curd, yet the curd does not arise from milk; if one understands that the nature of good and evil is inherently empty from the start, and does not seek to destroy evil by cultivating good, nor eliminate form to grasp emptiness, but simply cultivates immediate emptiness—this is the wisdom of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

If, from the very beginning, one is able to hear of the *amṛta* (ghee), and for the sake of the *amṛta*, milks the cow to obtain milk, boils the milk to make curd, transforms the curd into fresh butter (*navanīta*), and transforms the fresh butter into matured butter (*ghṛta*), only then obtaining the *amṛta*—to cultivate practice in this manner is the wisdom of the Separate Teaching.

If from the very beginning one had heard only that when the cow eats the *kṣānti-grass*, it produces *sarpis-maṇḍa* (ghee-essence), and if one were able to consume it, all ailments would be eliminated and all medicinal herbs would be contained therein.
To practice for this purpose is precisely the wisdom of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Regarding the "original" (*ben*) and the "traced" (*ji*): the original resides in the *prajñāpāramitā* of the true reality (*shixiang*), which serves as the mother; from the objective realm (*jing*) arises wisdom, wherein the realm is the body and wisdom is the child.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, the traced manifestation consists of the five flavors.
Śāriputra wished to transform the foul blood of afflictions into the wholesome milk of virtue, yet he manifested as an outsider possessing worldly wisdom, acting as a great master of treatises;
wishing to boil that milk into curd, he manifested the wisdom of the Tripiṭaka and became a second Buddha;
wishing to extract the cream from the curd, he spoke with stammering and displayed smallness, thereby accepting the humiliation of Vimalakīrti.
Desiring to transform raw butter into refined butter, he comforted and benefited his fellow practitioners of the same Brahma-faring; this was his reception of the teachings on Prajñāpāramitā.

Desiring to transform refined butter into the finest cream (amṛta), he attained initial awakening through the Lotus Sūtra. All of these were outward manifestations within his provisional traces, while his true ground remained inwardly secret for a long time.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: through the threefold contemplation within a single mind, one encompasses all wisdoms. Because the contemplation of the mind is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it encompasses the wisdom of curd;
because the contemplation of the mind is the provisional (*prajñapti*), it encompasses the wisdom of the two types of ghee as well as worldly wisdom;

because the contemplation of the mind is the Middle Way (*madhyamā*), it encompasses the wisdom of clarified butter (*sarpirmaṇḍa*). This is called, within the contemplation of the mind, "one wisdom is all wisdoms, all wisdoms are one wisdom, neither one wisdom nor all wisdoms," and so forth.
“Mahāmaudgalyāyana” is his clan name; it is translated as “Praise-Reciter. In the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, it is translated as “radish,” while Paramārtha states:
“Mudgara, which is translated here as ‘pea’; because these two things were the favorites of ancient seers, they named their clan after them.”
The *Śāstra* (Commentary) states:
"Jyotiṣka was the father of Siṃha; his name was Kauṣṭhila. 'Kauṣṭhila' is the name of a tree; because he obtained a son by praying to the deity of that tree, he was named after it."
Furthermore, regarding Maudgalyāyana, the *Anāgata-vaṃśa-sūtra* states:
"There are many who share the name Mahāmaudgalyāyana; therefore, 'the Great' is mentioned to distinguish him."

The *Śāstra* states: "Śāriputra was esteemed for his brilliant talent and insight, while Maudgalyāyana was valued for his noble and spirited character; their intellectual skills were comparable, and their virtuous conduct was identical."
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Among my disciples, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is foremost in those who, through supernatural powers, can levitate and fly to the ten directions."
The *Śāstra* (Treatise), fascicle 41, refers to him as the "disciple on the left.
Five hundred followers of a non-Buddhist teacher attempted to move a mountain using incantations; after one month, it had already begun to wobble and shake.
Maudgalyāyana thought to himself,
"If this mountain were to move, much harm would be done.
He immediately sat cross-legged in mid-air at the summit of the mountain, and the mountain remained motionless once more.
The non-Buddhists said to one another:
"The mountain of our doctrine has shaken; we calculated that it would surely shift within days. How is it that it remains so firm and solid, returning to its original state?
This must certainly have been caused by the śramaṇa."
Knowing his own strength was weak, he took refuge in the Buddha’s Way and led immeasurable people to leave the household life in accordance with the True Dharma.
As for "Nanda and Upananda," they were brothers who lived by the ocean at the edge of Mount Sumeru; the Buddha would often fly through the air to the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
This dragon was filled with resentment and anger, saying: "How can this shaven-headed man pass over me?
Later, when the Buddha wished to ascend to heaven, the dragon spat forth black clouds and dark mists, obscuring the three luminaries.
All the bhikṣus wished to subdue it, but the Buddha did not permit it.
Maudgalyāyana said,
"I am able to subdue this dragon."
The nāga coiled his body seven times around Mount Sumeru, with his tail thrust into the ocean and his head resting upon the mountain peak;
Maudgalyāyana manifested a body twice as large, coiling fourteen times around the mountain, with his tail extending beyond the sea and his head resting upon the Brahma palace.
The dragon’s anger intensified, and he rained down vajra-grit;
Maudgalyāyana transformed the grit into precious flowers, light, soft, and lovely to behold.
Yet the dragon’s wrath did not cease.

Maudgalyāyana transformed his body into a minute form and entered within the dragon’s body; he entered through the eyes and emerged from the ears, entered through the ears and emerged from the nose. As he bored and gnawed at its body, the dragon immediately experienced agonizing pain, and its mind was thereby subdued.
Maudgalyāyana, assuming a body both vast and minute, manifested the appearance of a śramaṇa and brought these two nāgas to the place where the Buddha was.

Devadatta led five hundred bhikṣus as his own followers; Maudgalyāyana grew weary of them and caused them to fall into a deep sleep, snoring and snorting like the roar of thunder, making sounds even below the wind. Although Kokālika stamped on them with his feet, they still did not wake. Śāriputra preached the Dharma and turned the hearts of the five hundred men; Maudgalyāyana then lifted them up with his hands and returned them, whereby the Sangha attained harmony.
Saṃyukta Āgama 29: “The Buddha was at Śrāvastī for the recitation of the precepts on the fifteenth day; the Buddha remained silent and did not speak.
Ānanda requested [him to speak] four times, and the Buddha said:”
"The assembly is not pure; I shall no longer recite the precepts.
You should have the Elder, or the one who upholds the Vinaya, or the one who recites the precepts, to proclaim them.

Maudgalyāyana immediately entered meditative concentration to observe who was impure. Seeing the two bhikṣus Aśvakarṇa and Pūrṇamāsa, he seized them by the hand and dragged them out. He then closed the door and again requested the Buddha to recite the precepts.
The Buddha said:
"I do not speak with duplicity; henceforth, I shall no longer recite the precepts myself.
Maudgalyāyana said:
"The assembly is not pure; I shall no longer serve as the *karmadāna*.

Regarding "Jīvaka," this is translated as "Life-Sustainer" (Gùhuó). He was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. When a disciple of Maudgalyāyana fell ill, Jīvaka traveled there by means of his supernatural powers to inquire after him. He encountered the devas leaving the garden to play; Jīvaka remained in his carriage without alighting, merely joining his palms in salutation.
Maudgalyāyana detained him, and Sengqu immediately said, "The devas enjoy their pleasures so busily that they have no leisure even to look at one another; what do you, Venerable One, seek?
He explained his purpose in coming in detail, to which [Sengqu] replied:
"Abstaining from food is the essential requirement.
When Maudgalyāyana released him, the chariot was finally able to move forward.

Śakra, having triumphed in battle against the asuras, constructed the Hall of Victory; its seven-jeweled towers and pavilions were magnificently adorned and extraordinary, with beams, pillars, and joints each capable of holding a single thread, supporting one another without touching—a testament to the wondrous power of celestial merit.

Maudgalyāyana flew there; Śakra led Maudgalyāyana to view the hall, whereupon all the celestial maidens were ashamed of Maudgalyāyana and hid themselves away, unable to come forth. Maudgalyāyana thought:
"Śakra is attached to pleasure and does not cultivate the root of the Path."

He immediately manifested a transformation that set the Hall of Victory ablaze; it collapsed in a brilliant conflagration. He then extensively expounded upon impermanence for Śakra, who was filled with joy. Afterwards, the hall remained solemn and intact, without a trace of ash or smoke.
Furthermore, as previously described, he placed five hundred Arhats in a net-bag. The Tathāgata’s Brahma-voice was deep and far-reaching;

even when heard from afar, it was no different than if one were at the Buddha’s side. Maudgalyāyana wished to know how far the Buddha’s voice extended, yet even when traveling to the utmost distances, he still heard it as if close at hand. He then used his supernormal powers to fly across lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the western direction, yet he heard the voice of the Lion of the Śākyas just as before, without change. Continuing on and on until his supernormal power was exhausted and his body was weary, he happened upon a great assembly in another region eating together.
He then rested upon the rim of a bowl and began to pace back and forth. Those people were struck with wonder and asked, "Whence has this head-worm come?"

That Buddha said: "This is the first disciple in spiritual power of the Buddha named Śākyamuni, who resides in an immeasurable Buddha-land to the east; he has followed the sound as far as this point, and it is not a worm."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"When the Buddha sought an attendant, his mind was set upon Ānanda, like the sun in the east shining upon a western wall," and so forth.

Regarding supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) from the perspective of the teachings: based on the fourteen transformations of the four dhyānas, and by relying on the cultivation through contemplation of the ten all-encompassing untainted (*anāsrava*) mundane meditations (*dhyāna*), one can perform the eighteen transformations; this constitutes the supernatural powers within the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*).

Relying on emptiness to give rise to wisdom, one cultivates the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) with a mind of empty wisdom; this is the supernormal power of the Shared Teaching (*samdhā-bhāṣita*).

By practicing and attaining supernormal powers in successive stages based on the three truths, one progressively penetrates deeper than the Two Vehicles; this is the supernormal power of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhāṣita*).

The supernormal powers attained by relying on the true nature of reality do not perceive the various Buddha-lands through dualistic characteristics; arising from the truth as responsive manifestations without wavering from the limit of reality, they pervade the ten Dharma-realms—this is the supernormal power of the Perfect Teaching, and so forth.
In the past, he once assisted a pratyekabuddha by shaving his head, washing and dyeing his robes, and sewing his *kāṣāya*; he then made a vow to attain supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), and so forth.

Regarding the "original" and the "traced": originally, he dwells in the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* at the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), able to respond universally to the ten directions in a single thought-moment, manifesting various forms to perform Buddha-works;
out of compassion, he traces himself through the supernatural powers of the five flavors of teaching to lead beings into the ultimate, and so forth.

As for the contemplation of the mind: one contemplates that within a single mind there suddenly arises all minds, and that all minds vanish in an instant so that no minds remain. Since the mind is neither existent nor non-existent, one penetrates to the true reality (bhūtatathatā); this is the contemplation of supernormal powers (abhijñā).

“Mahākātyāyana” is translated here as “Ornamented” (Wénshì) or “Shoulder-Borne” (Jiānshèng). Some say the character is erroneous and it should be read as “Fan-shéng” (Fanning Cord), meaning “Fine Shoulders. He is also named “Kāla,” which is translated as “Superior Thought” (Sīshèng); all these names are derived from his clan name.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"In skillfully discerning meanings and expounding the teachings of the Dharma, Kātyāyana is foremost. As the *Dīrgha Āgama* says:
"There was a non-Buddhist who clung to the view of annihilationism, asserting that there is no other world; there were ten rounds of questions and answers regarding this.
The non-Buddhist said:
'There is no other world.'"
He replied: "Are the sun and moon of this world or of another world? Are they celestial or human?"
"If there were no future world, there would be no tomorrow.
He asked again:
"I see people die and never return; how can you say they undergo suffering? Therefore, I know there is no future world."
He replied, "Suppose a criminal has been detained; would he be able to return?
He asked again:
"If you were born in heaven, why have you not returned?
Therefore, we know there is no other world. He replied:
"Suppose a person has fallen into a latrine and managed to escape; would they ever be willing to enter it again?

Furthermore, one day in heaven is equivalent to a hundred years here; if you were born there for only three or five days and had not yet found the opportunity to turn your heart toward the Way, even if someone from here were to return, you would have already passed away—how could you possibly know of it?"
He asked again:
"I boil sinners in cauldrons, covering them with tight lids; because I watch for it and do not see a spirit emerge, I know there is no other world."
He replied, "When you sleep during the day, do people standing beside you see your spirit leave your body?
He asked again:
"I flayed the skin from a dead man, cut the flesh into pieces, and crushed the bones, yet I could not find the spirit; therefore, I know there is no other world.
He replied, "It would be like a small child splitting firewood, seeking fire by breaking it into inch-long fragments—could fire ever be found in such a way?"
He asked again:
"When I weigh a dead person, they are heavier; if the spirit has departed, they should be lighter. If no spirit departs, then there is no other world. He replied:

"It is like when iron is combined with fire, the iron becomes light; when the iron loses the fire, it becomes heavy. When a person possesses the spirit (*śiva*), they are light; when they die and lose the spirit, they become heavy. He asked again:
"I have seen those on the verge of death who, upon turning back to seek their spirit, were unable to find it; therefore, I know there is no other world."
He replied: "It would be like a person turning a conch shell upside down in search of its sound; how could one ever obtain the sound?
He asked again:
"Although you have refuted it in various ways, I have clung to this for a very long time and cannot let it go.

He replied: "It is like a person gathering hemp: first seeing the hemp, they take the hemp; next they discard the hemp and take the bark; next they discard the bark and take the fibers; next they discard the fibers and take the cloth; next they discard the cloth and take the silk; next they discard the silk and take silver; next they discard the silver and take gold. Discarding the inferior to take the superior—how can one say they cannot let it go?"
He asked again:
"It is not only I who speak thus; all people also speak thus. Why do you claim that I am wrong? He replied:
Two merchants encountered a ghost who assumed a human form and said to them:
"The road ahead has abundant grain and sufficient fodder; why do you carry these?
One merchant immediately discarded his load. Consequently, the men and oxen on the road ahead all became hungry and were subsequently devoured by the ghost.
A merchant said: "If one obtains fresh rice-straw, one may discard the old rice-straw.
Thus, neither the person nor the ox was eaten by the ghosts.

The words of these people are false, like the deceptive speech of a ghost; since you did not accept my words, it was like discarding old rice and straw—now that you have obtained the new, why do you not discard the old?
He asked again:
"I cannot give it up; if you urge me to do so, I will become angry. He replied:

"You are like a pig-herder who, encountering excrement on the road, lifts it up with his head and carries it back. On the way, he encounters rain, and the liquid drips down, soiling his head. A bystander tells him to discard it, but instead of complying, he becomes angry at the man, saying, 'Because you do not raise pigs, you are making me discard this! Thus, he turns his anger toward the one who advised him."
As he thus analyzed and deconstructed each point in turn, extensively expounding upon various meanings, the non-Buddhist was eventually subdued and praised him, saying:
"Venerable One, I already understood what you previously said regarding the sun and moon; however, because I wished to hear your wisdom and eloquence, I repeatedly raised objections."
"Excellent! A wonderful exposition.
Kātyāyana’s skill in discussing the characteristics of doctrinal meaning was likewise thus.
The Vinaya states:

"One who is skillfully able to teach and transform others to take refuge in the precepts may cause a butcher to receive the night-precepts and a lecher to receive the day-precepts; later, when they receive their retribution, each will see the signs of pleasure before them during the day or the night, and so forth."
Furthermore, the Brahmin of worldly treatises said to the five hundred Śākyas,
"Are you able to debate with me?
The five hundred Śākyas replied:
"There was Godhika, who lacked wisdom and learning in his native land and whose speech was clumsy;
there was Cūḍapanthaka, who was also the lowest among those who had gone forth into homelessness."
"If you can defeat these two men in debate, I shall grant you the title of 'The Able One'.
Worldly Learning reflected:
"To defeat these two would not be particularly praiseworthy; however, if I were to fail, it would be a profound humiliation."
Later, he encountered Pāṇṭaka on the road and asked,
"What is your name? He replied:
"You should ask about the meaning; why trouble yourself to ask for the name?
He asked again, "Are you able to debate the meaning with me?"
He replied, "I am able to debate with the Brahma King; how much more so with you, a blind man without eyes?
He asked again:
"The blind have no eyes, and having no eyes is blindness; is this not redundant?
Zhouli performed eighteen transformations and then said, "This man can only perform feats of flight and transformation; he does not understand the meaning."
Kātyāyana heard this from afar with his divine ear; he immediately concealed Pāṇṭaka, manifested a body identical to his own, and descended from the air, asking:
"What is your name?"
He replied, “His name is Mahāpuruṣa.
He asked again:
"Is it not redundant to say that 'a man is a person' and 'a person is a man'?
The scholar replied: "Stop! [It is not so.]”
"Cease! Set aside these miscellaneous discussions; we may now discuss the profound meaning. He asked:
"Is it possible to attain nirvana without relying on the dharmas?
He replied:
"One can attain nirvana without relying on the dharmas of the five aggregates."
He asked again:
"Upon what do the five aggregates depend for their arising? He replied:
"It arises because of craving.
He asked again:
"How is craving abandoned?"
He replied:
"By relying on the Eightfold Noble Path, one can sever craving.
Upon hearing this, the worldly scholar was freed from dust and defilement.
Examples are all like this.

Regarding the exposition of meaning according to the teachings: to rely on impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self to refute views of annihilationism and eternalism is the exposition of meaning of the Initial Teaching.

Relying on emptiness, non-existence, and unattainability, one destroys those who cling to views of annihilationism or eternalism; this is the doctrinal exposition of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). Therefore, the goddess said:
"Because I have nothing to attain, my eloquence is such as this."

To rely on the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) and the dhāraṇīs, observing the capacities of beings and illuminating conventional designations to apply remedies according to their ailments, thereby shattering those with views of annihilationism or eternalism—this is the character of the doctrinal discourse of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekayāna*).

To rely on the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), which is neither existent nor non-existent, to shatter those with views of annihilationism or eternalism—this is the doctrinal discourse of the Perfect Teaching (*samyak-yāna*).
In terms of the fundamental and the manifested: fundamentally, he dwells in the two kinds of adornments—merit and wisdom—and is thus able to both question and answer;
yet, out of compassion for sentient beings, he manifests as a master of doctrinal discussion regarding the five flavors.

Regarding "contemplating the mind" (*guanxin*): it is the investigation of objects through contemplative wisdom; as objects arise from wisdom and wisdom engages with objects in a reciprocal process, this is precisely the exposition of the meaning of contemplating the mind.

"Aṇuruddha" is also called Aniruddha or Aniruddhu; these are merely variations in the transcription of the Sanskrit sound. Translated here, it means "Free from Poverty," "As One Wishes," or "Without Hunt"; these are its names.

In the past, during a time of famine, he offered wild millet rice to a Pratyekabuddha; as a result of this merit, he obtained sufficient rewards for ninety-one kalpas, and thus he was named "Non-Greed" (Alobha).

As for his clan name: at the beginning of the kalpa, when great waters prevailed, the wind blew and structured them to form the world. When the lifespan of those in the Ābhāsvara Heaven ended, they were reborn by transformation as humans. Their bodies possessed radiance, they traveled by flying, and they took joy as their sustenance. There were no distinctions of male or female, nor of noble or humble; because they were born together in such a multitude, they were called "sentient beings" (sattva).
The flavor of the earth-taste was like that of clarified butter (sarpis), its color like fresh ghee, and its sweetness like honey.

Those who ate much lost their radiance and became haggard, unable to fly; those who ate little remained lustrous. Thus, there arose competition and mutual criticism, which led to the loss of the earth-taste, and they began to eat the crust of the natural earth.
They began to treat one another with mutual contempt; consequently, they lost their skin and ate the earth’s surface.
As further evils arose, they lost their surface and ate naturally grown non-glutinous rice.
Upon eating this rice, male and female sexual organs developed, and they subsequently became husbands and wives.

Out of shame, they built houses and began to store up rice; later, the rice produced husks and chaff, and once harvested, it did not grow back, leaving only withered stalks visible. They then began to steal from one another, so they established a capable and impartial person as the Lord of the Fields to adjudicate disputes; this was the origin of the "Lord of Men" (Rājan).
The son of Mahāsammata was named Ratna; the son of Ratna was named Priyarasa.

From the time Mahāsammata first founded the kingdom, the Golden Wheel-turning Kings (Cakravartin) succeeded one another down to Suprabuddha. From King Māndhātṛ to Śuddhodana, there were four generations who ruled by the Iron Wheel; in total, there were eighty-four thousand two hundred and ten kings.
The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* states:
"In the distant past, there was a king who lost his parents at an early age. He entrusted the kingdom to his younger brother and served a brāhmaṇa."
The brāhmaṇa said, "You should change your royal robes and adopt the clan name Gautama.
He followed this advice, and people of the time called him Little Gautama; he then resided in the Ikṣuvāḍa grove.

A bandit passed by the garden with stolen goods; the pursuers followed his tracks, seized the Lesser Gautama, impaled him on a wooden stake, and shot him with arrows until blood flowed and stained the ground.
The Greater Gautama was filled with sorrow; he gathered the blood-stained earth, returned to the garden, placed it in a vessel, set it at his side, and recited this incantation:
"If this Gautama is sincere in heart, may the heavenly deity transform this blood back into a human being."
"Directly after ten months, a male was born on the left and a female on the right; from this they took the surname Gautama.
Gautama means "pure and refined"; it is also called Śākyan, and Śākyan refers to a noble clan.
At the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, when the Tathāgata Ratna appeared in the world, the *vijñāna* of Gautama first took conception.

If one traces this meaning, the Gautamas have been so surnamed since the time of the sovereigns. From the four sons of King Ambarīṣa—first, Ekacakṣu; second, Hastin; third, Mārgaṇa; and fourth, Alaṃkāra—they were suspected and exiled to the north of the Snowy Mountains into a forest of straight trees. Those of the nation who joyfully followed them gathered like a market, and they rose to become a powerful kingdom.
Their father, the king, sighed and said: "My son possesses great capability."
The four sons took this as their clan name.

Furthermore, the *śāka* trees in that land were extremely lush; this translates into Chinese as "Direct Forest" (*zhílín*). Since they established their kingdom within these forests, they took the forest as their clan name.

Foreign languages are often laden with hidden meanings, yet Śākyamuni was both direct and capable. As for the lineage currently upheld by Śuddhodana: he is a descendant of King Śobhita (Zhuāngyán). Śobhita is the same as Aṅga (Wūtóu); Aṅga fathered Aṅgīrasa (Wūtóuló); Aṅgīrasa fathered Nijūra (Níqiúluó); Nijūra fathered Siṃhahanu (Shīxiūluó), who is also known as Siṃhahanu (Shīzǐjiá). Siṃhahanu fathered three sons: Droṇodana (Sānfàn), Kṛkodara (Hùfàn), and Śuklodana. Of these two [latter] sons, the elder was named Mahānāman (Móhénán) and the younger was Aniruddha (Ānàlǜ). Thus, [Śuddhodana] is the nephew of King Śuddhodana, the second son of King Kṛkodara, the first cousin of the World-Honored One, the elder brother of Ānanda, and the uncle of Rāhula; he is certainly no ordinary man.
Therefore, the Duke of Zhou sighed and said:

"I am the son of King Wen, the younger brother of King Wu, and the uncle of King Cheng; I am no lowly man in this world. Yet he bathed me three times after grasping my hand and made me eat three times before spitting out the food. If such was the treatment accorded to one who values the worthy, how much more so for others?"
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states:

"During the period of the Dharma-ending age of Buddha Puṣya, there was a famine in the world. A pratyekabuddha named Liṭa went begging but returned with an empty bowl, having obtained nothing. A poor man saw him and felt deep compassion, saying:
'Noble sir, would you be able to accept some millet?'"
He immediately offered her what he had been eating.
After she had eaten, he performed the eighteen transformations.
Later, while gathering wild millet, a rabbit leaped up and embraced his back; it transformed into a corpse, and having no companion, he was able to escape.

When he waited for darkness to return home, [the objects] that lay upon the ground immediately became golden figures; as he pulled out his fingers, they grew back accordingly, and as he used his feet, more emerged, such that taking them was inexhaustible.

When wicked men and evil kings came wishing to seize them, they saw only corpses, yet what he beheld were purely gold and jewels. Having fully realized the karmic retribution of ninety-one kalpas, he was thus named "The One Without Poverty" (Aparājita).

After his birth, the family’s wealth became abundant and increased day and night. His parents, wishing to test him, sent off an empty vessel covered over; when it was opened, it was found to be filled with a hundred flavors.
Under his guidance, there were always twelve thousand people every day: six thousand who took loans and six thousand who returned the principal.
After he had left the household life, wherever he went, people saw him with joy; whatever they wished to obtain, it was no different from being in their own homes.
Anuruddha was so diligent that for seven days and seven nights his eyelids did not blink; since sleep is the nourishment of the eyes, having not slept for seven days, his eyes lost their vision.

Having lost his physical eye, the Buddha instructed him to seek the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Fixing his mindfulness upon its object, a pure form derived from the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) emerged, covering half his head. It penetrated all obstructions, both internal and external, and he beheld all things, whether light or dark. Addressing the Brahmā King, he said:
"I see Śākyamuni’s trichiliocosm as clearly as if I were looking at a fruit in the palm of my hand."
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"In my Buddha-dharma, as for those with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) who see through all things, the bhikṣu Aniruddha is foremost.

Since Aniruddha had lost his physical eyes, the Buddha and the bhikṣus would constantly perform tailoring for him. Once, while the Buddha was at the Kausāmbī Cave in Śrāvastī, he gathered eight hundred bhikṣus to make three robes (*tricīvara*) for Aniruddha. The Buddha himself stretched out the fabric, while the bhikṣus cut and sewed; thus, they were completed in a single day.
