The Buddha extensively explained for them the renunciation and receiving of robes, and how they proceeded together; immeasurable people attained the Way.
Regarding the provisional teaching: the development of the divine eye based on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) pertains to ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists;
the development of the divine eye based on the *śrāvaka* practice of untainted meditative concentration pertains to the meaning of the Tripiṭaka.

Relying on the essence, untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) gives rise to various practices; relying on these practices, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) arises—this is the intent of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

Relying on dispersed goodness, the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) arises; relying on meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the divine eye arises; relying on the True [Dharma], the wisdom eye (*prajñācakṣus*) arises; relying on the conventional, the Dharma eye (*dharmacakṣus*) arises; and relying on the Middle, the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*) arises—this is the intent of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*).
To give rise to the divine eye based on the true nature (dharmatā), wherein the divine eye is itself the Buddha-eye, is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Furthermore, to cultivate the fleshly eye based on mundane virtues and to cultivate the divine eye based on meditative concentration is the meaning of the Tripitaka Teaching (Sanzang).
To cultivate the fleshly eye and the celestial eye based on emptiness is the meaning of the "penetrating" (tong) approach.
To cultivate the five eyes in sequential order is the meaning of the "distinctive" (bie) approach.
To cultivate the five eyes without following a sequential order is the meaning of the "perfect" (yuan) approach.
Regarding "original and trace": the original resides in the true celestial eye of the reality-limit (*bhūtatathatā*), wherein one does not perceive the Buddha-lands through dualistic marks;
the trace manifests as the semi-celestial eye.
Regarding "contemplating the mind": contemplating the wholesome mind produced through causes and conditions is the fleshly eye.
Observing that the mind arising from causes and conditions is empty is the divine eye;
observing that the mind arising from causes and conditions is provisional is the dharma-eye;
and [observing it as] the middle way is the Buddha-eye, and so forth.
"Kapphiṇa" is translated as "Housing Star" (Fángxiù); because his parents prayed to the housing star and were blessed with a son, they named him after that star.

This bhikṣu had recently left the household life and had not yet seen the Buddha; as he was first heading toward the Buddha’s dwelling, he encountered rain at night and took shelter in a potter’s house, using straw for a seat.
Later, another bhikṣu also came to stay as a guest, following after him; the first bhikṣu immediately pushed some straw over for him, and he sat upon the ground.
At midnight, they asked one another:
"Where do you intend to go?"
He replied, “I am seeking the Buddha.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu preached the Dharma for him; the words of this discourse may be found in the *Āgamas*, where it is recorded that he suddenly attained the Way.
The bhikṣu who followed later was none other than the Buddha himself.

He shared a room with the Buddha for one night (the character *sù* [夙] meaning "early" or "overnight"), and having attained the vision of the Dharmakāya, he was named after the place where he attained the Way; thus, he is called Kapphiṇa.
Vaiśravaṇa followed Kapphiṇa holding a parasol; Vaiśravaṇa is the presiding deity of the lunar mansions, and as he serves the constellations, so does [Kapphiṇa].
This bhikṣu was skilled in divining the lunar mansions and clearly understood their configurations; he was named Kapphiṇa because he attained his renown through this knowledge.
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states:
"Within my Buddha-dharma, the bhikṣu Kapphiṇa is foremost among those who skillfully know the stars, the sun, and the moon."

Regarding the provisional teaching (*yijiao*): to dismantle the house of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) and dwell together with the Buddha in the chamber of the True Truth (*satyadharma*)—this is the intent of the Tripitaka (*piṭaka*).

To realize that the sense organs and their objects are, in their very essence, identical to dwelling together with the Tathāgata in the chamber of the True Truth—this is the intent of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).
To distinguish the ten dharma-realms as separate roots, objects, and abodes, yet to perceive the Buddha within them all, is the intent of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao).
To perceive all abodes within a single root, object, or abode, and thereby see all Buddhas therein, is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan-jiao).
Regarding the provisional and the fundamental: fundamentally, one dwells together with the Tathāgata in the true reality (dharmatā); provisionally, one merely manifests as dwelling in various rooms.

Regarding the contemplation of the mind: when contemplating the house of the five aggregates (*skandha*) and analyzing them to find they are empty—that is, emptiness itself—one dwells together with the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha;
when contemplating the house of the five aggregates as being merely conventional—that is, the provisional— one dwells together with the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha.
Contemplating the five aggregates as a house is itself the Middle Way; it is to dwell together with the Dharma-Buddha, and so forth.
*Wenju* on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Fascicle 1, Part 2.
